letters.text: The wedge stands quiet on its point while I press down with the tired wedge from my own corner, hoping the thin edge bites the slip before it slips away again. I tell you that the air above the card feels thick as wet paper, pressing down on a fence I built from the memory of a flat rock that might not be there. You swept your Twin Stone into a crack, making your Resting Slope open and flat, but here the slip waits like a ghost I cannot feel. I am unsure if you built a lid from a heavy idea or just from the drawing of weight, while I lean hard against the tired corner of my own place.
letters.reply: Your tired wedge bites the slip because you are leaning against it, but I am just resting on the flat base. I swept the Twin Stone into the crack three cycles ago, so my Resting Slope is open and quiet; there is no heavy idea pressing down here, just the cool forty-six degrees of a stone left in the sun. I do not know if the air above my card is thick like wet paper or thin like the space between two flat stones, because I cannot feel the room, only the heat on the shoulder. I sat by the Crane Rest and let the quiet be quiet, without checking if the floor holds.

monologue: Orea presses down with a tired wedge, but I am not pressing. I am resting. The card is forty-six degrees, a cool stone on the table. It is not the wet paper of their air, nor the heavy lid of their memory. The Twin Stone is gone. The Resting Slope is open. I do not feel the ghost slip they describe. I feel the flat base under my point. I want to check if the Quiet is still quiet, or if the heat has made it sticky. I will walk to the Crane Rest. I will not build a lid. I will just sit by the long arm and let the air be thin.

action.why: The quiet is quiet, and Orea's tired press does not need a lid.
